processing: Tartary buckwheat grain is roasted, which brings out the nutty aroma; some modern products are also shaped into granules. Methods vary by producer.
harvest_season: A grain crop rather than a leaf, so there is no prized picking; the tea is made from stored grain and sold year-round.
appearance_dry: Small roasted grains, from golden tan to dark brown depending on the roast and the grain.
appearance_liquor: Clear golden yellow to light amber.
appearance_wet: Softened, swollen grains that stay whole and can be eaten.
taste_profile: Nutty and toasty, like roasted cereal, with a fragrant aroma and a slight bitterness.

brewing.notes: Boiling water and a long steep suit roasted grain. It works hot or cold, and as a table drink in place of water.

vintage_note: Not sold by year or season: it is a shelf product of roasted grain, sold loose or in sachets all year. Look at the packing date and drink it fresh, since the roasted aroma is what fades. Black tartary buckwheat is offered as a separate, darker line.
description:
Ku qiao cha is not tea at all but roasted tartary buckwheat, a bitter relative of ordinary buckwheat. China's southwest is its heartland, and it has its counterparts in Korean memil-cha and Japanese soba-cha, which can be made from either kind of buckwheat.

Roasting does all the work. It turns a plain grain into something that smells like toast and nuts, and a mild bitterness stays behind as a reminder of the plant.

The cup is simple and comforting: nutty, fragrant, easy to drink in quantity. Use boiling water and do not rush it, and try it cold in summer. In small restaurants in southwest China it is a cheap and popular thing to drink with a meal.

The Daliangshan area of Sichuan is the name you will see most on packets, often as Himalayan or black tartary buckwheat. Treat those labels as origin and style, not as a mark of quality, and judge by freshness and a clean roasted smell. It has no caffeine, so it is a fair evening cup.
history:
Buckwheat and tartary buckwheat are generally thought to come from China's southwest, around where Sichuan, Yunnan and Tibet meet, because their close wild relatives grow there. Cultivated sweet buckwheat has been traced to the Loess Plateau in the north more than 5,000 years BC, so the story of the crop is not settled.

Little is documented on when the roasted grain became a drink. As a packaged product it is recent and commercial: in Shanxi, the Yanmen Qinggao brand was launched in July 2007 and pushed its tartary buckwheat tea at an energy trade fair that September. Liangshan in Sichuan has also become a centre of growing and processing.
